issues.legal_issue: The executive government may reorganize local administrative areas, abolish an existing area and its local body, and establish new areas and bodies when the legislature has conferred that power.
material_facts: Government notifications divided rural areas into new administrative units, abolished the unit associated with the appellant’s local body, and brought that body’s term to an end.

The governing enactment empowered the government to modify the areas of existing units and create new units; related provisions addressed the consequences of units ceasing to exist and the termination of local bodies’ terms.
issues.conclusion: The notifications flowed from an express grant of legislative power and were valid exercises of that power.
issues.legal_principle: The Court read the power to create and modify administrative units together with the power, reflected in the related provisions, to abolish old units and create new ones. Sections 3, 4, 8 and 8A of the Uttar Pradesh Kshettra Samities and Zila Parishads Adhiniyam, 1961 authorized reorganization and termination in connection with that reorganization.

predicates.challenge_to_local_area_reorganization: A person challenges government action that reorganizes local administrative areas.
predicates.government_can_modify_area_boundaries: The governing law authorizes the government to alter the boundaries of existing local administrative areas.
predicates.government_can_create_new_areas: The governing law authorizes the government to establish new local administrative areas.

issues.definition: When a challenge concerns local-area reorganization and the government is authorized to modify boundaries and create new areas, the reorganization is within executive authority.

issues.legal_issue: A local body's corporate status and perpetual succession do not guarantee the continued existence of that particular body or prevent its abolition through a legally authorized reorganization.
material_facts: The appellant argued that the local body’s corporate status, perpetual succession, property, funds, and contemplated term prevented the government from abolishing it.
The enactment also empowered the government to reorganize the areas for which local bodies were established.
issues.conclusion: Perpetual succession did not entail the perpetual existence of any particular local body or administrative area, and the provisions governing the body's functions while it existed did not impair the power to reorganize areas.
issues.legal_principle: The Court distinguished succession from perpetual existence: perpetual succession permits one body to succeed another but does not prevent the abolition of a particular body for valid administrative reasons. The provisions governing incorporation, property, funds, and terms apply while a body continues; they do not negate the reorganization powers under sections 3, 4, 8 and 8A of the Uttar Pradesh Kshettra Samities and Zila Parishads Adhiniyam, 1961.

predicates.challenge_to_local_body_abolition: A person challenges the abolition of a local body established for an administrative area.
predicates.local_body_has_perpetual_succession: The local body has corporate status and perpetual succession.
predicates.law_authorizes_area_reorganization: The governing law authorizes the government to reorganize the administrative areas served by local bodies.

issues.definition: When an abolished local body has perpetual succession but the law authorizes reorganization of its area, perpetual succession does not prevent abolition.

issues.legal_issue: Delegating decisions about the size, boundaries, and number of local administrative areas to the executive is not excessive when the legislation states its policy and supplies guidance for those decisions.
material_facts: The appellant argued that the law gave the government unguided power to create and reorganize administrative areas.

The enactment stated its democratic and administrative objectives, described the purposes and duties of local bodies, and left choices about area size, territory, and number of bodies to the government.
The Court considered those choices appropriate for executive determination in light of local wishes, political exigencies, and administrative needs.
issues.conclusion: The enactment did not confer unfettered or uncanalized power, and the delegation was valid.
issues.legal_principle: The legislative policy and objectives may be ascertained from the preamble and other provisions, and the legislature may leave implementation details to the executive when it has sufficiently expressed its policy and supplied guidance. The Court followed State of Bhopal v. Champalal, [1964] 6 S.C.R. 35.

predicates.challenge_to_legislative_delegation: A person challenges legislation on the ground that it delegates legislative power to the executive.
predicates.legislation_states_policy_and_objectives: The legislation states its underlying policy and the objectives the executive is to implement.
predicates.executive_choices_are_implementation_det: The executive choices concern practical details of implementation, such as the size, territory, or number of local administrative areas.

issues.definition: When legislation states its policy and objectives and leaves only implementation details to the executive, a challenge to that delegation does not succeed.

issues.legal_issue: A law permitting reorganization of local administrative areas does not violate equality merely because reorganization results in the departure of local representatives, unless the reorganization is used as a direct means to remove them.
material_facts: The appellant argued that the reorganization power provided an indirect means to remove local representatives without using the law's removal procedures.
The Court found that reorganization and removal were distinct powers directed at different subjects.
The appellant alleged bad faith, but no material established that the reorganization was undertaken to remove a representative; the findings below rejected that allegation.
The Court distinguished Ram Dial v. State of Punjab, [1965] 2 S.C.R. 858, where alternative procedures directly concerned removal and created scope for arbitrary choice.
issues.conclusion: The challenged provisions did not violate Article 14. A reorganization undertaken directly to remove a representative could be struck down as mala fide, but no such purpose was established in this case.
issues.legal_principle: Article 14 does not require comparing powers that operate in distinct fields, such as direct removal of representatives and reorganization of administrative areas. Reorganization may be invalid if it is used mala fide for the direct purpose of removing a representative. Ram Dial v. State of Punjab, [1965] 2 S.C.R. 858, was distinguished.

predicates.equality_challenge_to_local_area_reorgan: A person challenges local-area reorganization on the ground that it indirectly removes local representatives.
predicates.reorganization_power_differs_from_direct: The power used reorganizes administrative areas, while a separate power directly governs removal of local representatives.
predicates.evidence_of_reorganization_to_remove_rep: Evidence shows that the reorganization was undertaken for the direct purpose of removing a local representative.

issues.definition: When an equality challenge concerns reorganization under a power distinct from direct removal, and there is no evidence that reorganization was used to remove a representative, the reorganization does not violate the equality guarantee.
